name: Neoliberalism
info: Neoliberalism is a political and economic ideology that advocates free-market capitalism; it arose among European liberal scholars in the 1930s, shaped policy from the late 20th century, and remains a contested, often pejorative term.

facts.thinkers: Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises, who held that the state's only legitimate role was to abolish barriers to market entry; Walter Lippmann, Alexander Rüstow and Wilhelm Röpke, who favoured strong state supervision of the economy; Walter Eucken and Alfred Müller-Armack of the German social market economy; Milton Friedman, founder of monetarism; George Stigler and James M. Buchanan
facts.texts: Walter Lippmann’s An Inquiry into the Principles of the Good Society; Milton Friedman’s essay “Neo-Liberalism and its Prospects” (1951) and Capitalism and Freedom; Friedrich Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom; Charles Peters’s “A Neoliberal’s Manifesto” (1983); John Williamson’s ten rules of the Washington Consensus (1989)
facts.ideas: the priority of the price mechanism; free enterprise and competition; privatisation; deregulation; free trade; monetarism and price stability; lower taxes and reduced government spending; economic and political freedom as linked
facts.today: Neoliberal policies are associated with governments in Chile, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, New Zealand and many others from the 1970s and 1980s, and with the IMF and World Bank; the term is used mainly by critics and is largely absent from economics journals, while the Adam Smith Institute changed its label from libertarian to neoliberal in 2016

t: The term was chosen in 1938 at the Walter Lippmann Colloquium in Paris, where its founders agreed that laissez-faire liberalism had failed but disagreed sharply over how strong the state should be.

Its policies were widely implemented only after the economic crises of the 1970s, first in Chile under Augusto Pinochet’s military junta, then under Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, and then abroad through IMF and World Bank loan conditions.
Scholars dispute what the word means: it is often used pejoratively and rarely by proponents of free-market policies, and some scholars call it an essentially contested concept.
dyk: At the 1938 Colloquium that named neoliberalism, Ludwig von Mises denounced the ordoliberalism of the rival faction as “ordo-interventionism”, while Alexander Rüstow wrote that Hayek and Mises were relics of the liberalism that caused the Great Depression.
ev: The French economist Charles Gide uses the term in English to describe the beliefs of the Italian economist Maffeo Pantaleoni
The Walter Lippmann Colloquium meets in Paris and chooses “neoliberalism” as the name of a new liberal project
The Mont Pelerin Society is founded, with Hayek, Friedman, Popper, Stigler and Mises among its founding members
A coup in Chile establishes the military junta of Augusto Pinochet, which later adopts the Chicago Boys’ reforms
Margaret Thatcher becomes Conservative prime minister, a post she holds until 1990
Congress follows Reagan’s proposal and cuts United States federal income taxes across the board by 25%
David Lange appoints Roger Douglas finance minister in New Zealand, beginning the reforms known as Rogernomics

sections.origins:
Neoliberalism originated among European liberal scholars during the 1930s, as a response to the perceived decline in popularity of classical liberalism, which was seen as giving way to a social liberal desire to control markets. An early use of the term in English came in 1898 from the French economist Charles Gide, who applied it to the economic beliefs of the Italian economist Maffeo Pantaleoni; the term néo-libéralisme already existed in French.

In August 1938 twenty-five liberal intellectuals, among them Walter Lippmann, Friedrich Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, Wilhelm Röpke, Alexander Rüstow and Louis Rougier, met in Paris at the Walter Lippmann Colloquium, held to mark the French translation of Lippmann’s An Inquiry into the Principles of the Good Society. They called for a new liberal project and chose “neoliberalism”, one name among several floated, defining it as involving “the priority of the price mechanism, free enterprise, the system of competition, and a strong and impartial state”. Most agreed that laissez-faire liberalism had failed, but they disagreed deeply on the state’s role: a group around Rüstow and Lippmann advocated strong state supervision of the economy, while Mises and Hayek insisted that the only legitimate role for the state was to abolish barriers to market entry.

Divided and short of funds, the Colloquium was mostly ineffectual and was overwhelmed by the outbreak of the Second World War. It nonetheless served as the first meeting of the nascent movement and as the precursor to the Mont Pelerin Society.
sections.ideas:
Neoliberal thinkers differed over what they proposed. In his early essay “Neo-Liberalism and Its Prospects”, Milton Friedman wrote that neoliberalism would accept the nineteenth-century liberal emphasis on the individual but substitute for laissez-faire the goal of “the competitive order”, which requires limited state intervention to “police the system, establish conditions favorable to competition and prevent monopoly, provide a stable monetary framework, and relieve acute misery and distress”. By the 1970s neoliberal thought, Friedman’s included, focused almost exclusively on market liberalisation and opposed nearly all state interference in the economy.

Its policies centre on economic liberalisation: reductions to trade barriers, deregulation of industry, privatisation of state-owned enterprises, reductions in government spending and monetarism. Neoliberal theory contends that free markets encourage efficiency, growth and innovation, and state intervention is generally believed to worsen economic performance. Monetarism, formulated by Friedman, holds that excessive expansion of the money supply is inflationary and that monetary authorities should focus on price stability.

Many neoliberal thinkers hold that economic and political freedom are linked. Friedman argued in Capitalism and Freedom that economic freedom is a necessary condition for political freedom; Hayek wrote in The Road to Serfdom that “Economic control is not merely control of a sector of human life which can be separated from the rest; it is the control of the means for all our ends”.
sections.spread:
Neoliberalism began accelerating in importance with the establishment of the Mont Pelerin Society in 1947. For decades its ideas stayed largely on the fringes of policy, confined to think-tanks and universities, with measured success only among the ordoliberals in Germany. There the economists around Ludwig Erhard drew on theories developed in the 1930s and 1940s, and Alfred Müller-Armack coined the phrase “social market economy”. In Germany neoliberalism at first meant both ordoliberalism and the social market economy, but the original term gradually disappeared as the latter fitted better with the Wirtschaftswunder mentality of the 1950s and 1960s.

It was not until a succession of economic downturns and crises in the 1970s that neoliberal proposals were widely implemented. The Reagan administration and Thatcher government began neoliberal reforms in the early 1980s to counter the stagflation each country had experienced in the 1970s, and policies of this kind were then exported to Latin America, the Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and China. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank encouraged reform in many developing countries by placing requirements on loans, a process known as structural adjustment, whose principles became known as the Washington Consensus.

A “second wave” followed in the 1990s: Bill Clinton and Tony Blair, identifying with a moderate position known as the Third Way, embraced a neoliberal ideology. Some scholars say the rise of neoliberalism around the world began when the Soviet Union dissolved and the Cold War ended.
sections.power:
Chile was among the earliest nations to adopt neoliberal reform. After a 1973 coup overthrew President Salvador Allende, a military junta under Augusto Pinochet, known for its violent suppression of opposition, gave the Chicago Boys, Chilean economists who had studied under Milton Friedman, significant political influence. They carried out rapid privatisation of state enterprises, deregulation and reductions in trade barriers, and the central bank raised interest rates from 49.9% to 178%. Inflation fell from over 600% in 1974 to below 50% by 1979, but inequality widened. After a severe recession in 1982 the economy grew quickly; Friedman called the period the “Miracle of Chile”, while some scholars call it a failure that led to extreme inequalities. Alejandro Foxley states that around 44% of Chilean families lived below the poverty line when Pinochet left office in 1990.

In the United Kingdom, Margaret Thatcher’s governments from 1979 to 1990 reduced taxes, deregulated and privatised, and reduced the power of trade unions. In the United States, Reagan’s administration cut taxes and deregulated finance, and the Clinton administration passed NAFTA and repealed the Glass–Steagall Act.

In Argentina the military dictatorship’s 1976 programme froze salaries, and poverty rose from 9% in 1975 to 40% at the end of 1982. In Peru, Alberto Fujimori adopted aggressive neoliberal policies after taking office in 1990, and at least 300,000 Peruvians were victims of forced sterilisation by his government in the 1990s.
sections.critiques:
Critics include economists Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen, Ha-Joon Chang and Thomas Piketty, the linguist Noam Chomsky, the geographer David Harvey and Pope Francis. Harvey describes neoliberalism as a “class project” designed to increase the class power of economic elites; Wendy Brown asserts that its overriding objective is “the economization of all features of life”; Paul Krugman argues that the “laissez-faire absolutism” promoted by neoliberals fostered an intellectual climate in which faith in markets often trumps the evidence. Loïc Wacquant and Bernard Harcourt link mass incarceration in the United States to neoliberal policy, and Pope Francis called unfettered capitalism “a new tyranny”.

A 2016 IMF paper found “much to cheer in the neoliberal agenda” but concluded that freedom of capital and fiscal consolidation resulted in increasing inequality, and that the benefits in growth were difficult to establish. Kristen Ghodsee argues that neoliberal capitalism left economic misery in the former Eastern Bloc and fuelled a resurgence of extremist nationalism.

Critics also come from the free-market side. Sheldon Richman argues that the IMF imposed a “corporatist-flavored ‘neoliberalism’”, and Mises accused the German neoliberals of “ordo-interventionism”. Will Hutton called the word “an unthinking leftist insult”, and Daniel Stedman Jones says it is too often a catch-all shorthand for the horrors associated with globalisation and financial crises.
sections.legacy:
The term entered common academic use in the 1980s in association with Pinochet’s reforms in Chile, quickly acquired negative connotations, and by 1994 had entered global circulation. One study of 148 scholarly articles found it almost never defined. Scholars therefore describe it as an essentially contested concept; some, such as Gary Gerstle, hold that it remains a meaningful term, and Stephen Metcalf argues that the 2016 IMF paper helps put to rest the idea that it is merely a slur. Gerstle writes that Reagan was the ideological architect of the neoliberal order and Clinton its key facilitator.

The Great Recession of 2008 gave rise to a surge of scholarship critical of neoliberalism. Political opposition from the late 1990s onward included the “pink tide” of leftist governments in Latin America, the yellow vests protests in France in 2018 and the Chilean protests of 2019–2021. During the 2021 Chilean general election Gabriel Boric promised to end the country’s neoliberal economic model, stating that “if Chile was the cradle of neoliberalism, it will also be its grave”. Adam Kotsko describes neoliberalism as a political theology that aspires to be a complete way of life.

Neoliberalism has been a significant factor in the proliferation of conservative and right-libertarian organisations, parties and think-tanks, which predominantly advocate it. The term remains largely absent from economics journals.

summary: Neoliberalism is a free-market ideology named at a 1938 Paris colloquium and spread by the Mont Pelerin Society. Its policies were widely applied from the 1970s, in Chile under Pinochet, in Britain and the United States, and through the IMF and World Bank. Scholars dispute the term, which is often pejorative.

notes: Start 1938, circa false: the Walter Lippmann Colloquium of August 1938 chose the name; the article also gives 1898 for Gide's early use in English and says neoliberalism 'originated among European liberal scholars during the 1930s'.

The article contradicts itself on the coining of the label: it says the Colloquium chose the term among others floated, but also that Rüstow 'had coined the label neoliberalism'. I wrote only that the Colloquium chose it and left out the Rüstow claim.
Region 'Americas' as given, although the article places the origins in Europe (Paris, Vienna, Freiburg).
Article says Colloquium attendees numbered 25; the Mont Pelerin Society's founding members 'included' the five named, so I wrote 'among its founding members'.

The Peru section links Fujimori's sterilisations to USAID support through a source (Foundation for Economic Education) and says the policies 'resulted in' impoverishment; I wrote only the 300,000 figure as the article states it and left out the allegations about funders and the Plan Verde passage, which are long and contested.

Chile figures: the article gives mixed and partly conflicting poverty figures (50% in 1984 to 34% in 1989; 44% of families in 1990; 17% in 1969 to 45% in 1985). I kept only Foxley's 44% attributed to him and the inflation figures; the article's 'inflation below 10% before 1982' and GDP growth of 10% are left out.
The article calls the 1973 coup 'instigated by the United States'; I wrote only 'a 1973 coup' because the same article elsewhere says 'diplomatic, economic, and covert pressure'.
The article says Chile's 1980 plebiscite and constitution were controversial; left out for length.

Left out: national sections on Mexico, Brazil, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, China, the Middle East and the EU; the Austrian, Chicago and Geneva schools; Nixon and Carter administrations; Powell memorandum; global health, environment, financialisation and imperialism critiques (Blakeley on Indonesia); the 'Atari Democrats'.

Facts 'thinkers' lists James M. Buchanan and George Stigler from the article's lists of associated figures; the article gives no word on each, so the descriptions come from the article's own statements on factions and the monetarism section.
The 'today' fact on the Adam Smith Institute uses the article's date, October 2016.
